questions.q: What are the four sections of the ADR format taught in this lesson, in order?
options: Context, Options Considered, Decision, Consequences
Summary, Requirements, Architecture, Appendix
Problem, Stakeholders, Timeline, Budget
Overview, Risks, Decision, Sign-off
questions.explain: The format that has stuck across teams is Context (why a decision was needed), Options Considered (the real alternatives), Decision (what was chosen), and Consequences (the resulting tradeoffs, upsides and downsides both).

questions.q: Why does this lesson say listing only the winning option, with no rejected alternatives, is a common way ADRs fail?
options: It violates a formal ISO documentation standard
It makes the Markdown file too short to render correctly
A reader later on can't tell whether a changed circumstance should reopen a question that was never actually shown to be considered against alternatives
Cloud providers require at least three listed options per decision
questions.explain: Without the rejected alternatives recorded, a reader has no way to judge whether circumstances have changed enough that the original tradeoff should be reconsidered.

questions.q: In the worked ADR-0012 example, what specific downside does the Consequences section honestly record about the hub-and-spoke decision?
options: That hub-and-spoke is more expensive than full mesh peering in every case
That the hub becomes a single point of contention for network throughput within a region, plus an added hop of under 2ms of latency
That hub-and-spoke cannot support more than two regions
That the compliance team rejected the hub-and-spoke design outright
questions.explain: The Consequences section names the real tradeoffs accepted: the hub as a bandwidth chokepoint to monitor, and a measured latency cost of under 2ms per spoke-to-spoke hop through the hub.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a Consequences section that reads "all upside" actually signals?
options: That the decision was clearly the correct one with no risk at all
That the team used an outdated ADR template
That the ADR should be deleted and rewritten from scratch
That the tradeoff either wasn't real or wasn't honestly recorded, since every meaningful architecture decision has some downside
questions.explain: An ADR whose Consequences section lists only benefits reads like marketing copy rather than an honest record of a tradeoff — real architecture decisions always carry some accepted downside.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Status field (Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, or Superseded by ADR-XXXX) mentioned in this lesson?
options: It records which cloud provider hosts the resulting infrastructure
It lets a reader immediately tell whether the ADR still reflects the current design, without having to ask anyone
It is a legal requirement for infrastructure-as-code repositories
It determines the file's sort order in the repository only
questions.explain: The Status field tells a reader at a glance whether the decision recorded is still in force, was never finalized, or has been replaced — which matters as the architecture evolves over time.
